Why an operating system, and why now
The stack is a bet about where the hard part of AI moved: from the demo to the production run, and from one vendor to five.

Agents turned one user action into many model calls, so who holds the keys, what each key may spend and what happens when a provider degrades became production questions rather than operational details.

Open-weight models became good enough for narrow, repeated tasks, so the data a team owns and the GPUs it already rents started to matter more than which vendor it calls. And procurement caught up: a legal review now asks where prompts go before an engineer asks whether the model works.
These layers belong together, the way Unix's did

The file system, the data, the models, the gateway and the agents are bought today from five vendors under five contracts, with scripts for glue. Runix draws them once and builds each as a product a team can adopt on its own.

The company that keeps the layers honest with each other, under one contract, one call interface and the customer's own storage and compute, earns the position an operating system has: everything above it can change without touching anything beneath.
In the order the evidence allows

The gateway is available today. The file system, the data and the models are in early access. The agents are in development. Nothing on this site is marked further along than it is, and a build check fails the site if any page disagrees with the product list.

What is in writing is linked, not promised: data terms, contracting, the price catalogue and the roadmap. Three of the tools we built to run a gateway are open source, including a benchmark you can run against us.
And we build it AI-native. Agents write, test and operate most of this stack, under human review, and they face the same gates a person would: a change that breaks a check does not ship.

Five questions, in the order they matter

A team picking a gateway asks whether it can trust it, then whether it is cheap, then whether it stays up. The benchmark answers in that order, and reads a low price next to trust: a gateway far under list price is a warning sign, not a bargain.

Is it the real model, and will the operator still be there? A fixed request set goes to the gateway and to the official API at once, following the K2 Vendor Verifier method, and the answers are compared. Data retention and the legal entity are annotated with links to the source.
The gateway's price divided by the official list price, per model and as one index across models. Cache pricing and hidden multipliers are recorded beside it.
Success rate from a probe every six hours, with rate limits, outages and timeouts counted apart. Errors the probe causes itself, such as an unauthorised key, are excluded and shown separately.

Time to first token at p50, and p95 only when a run has at least five samples. Throughput is counted after the first token, the convention llmperf and Artificial Analysis use. Fake streaming, a reply buffered and then dumped, is flagged.
Whether a repeated prompt is billed and served as a cache hit, measured rather than taken from the price page.
Each claim is verified, claimed but unverified, or unverified. Nothing without an evidence link is ever marked verified, and a related party is never rated a tier higher for the relationship.
Where it sits, and how it measures
The benchmark stands where your application stands: outside the gateway, calling its public endpoint. It needs no access to anyone's infrastructure and no cooperation from the operator.

The probe script and its prompts are in the repository. Each request carries a random id so a gateway cannot serve it from a cache, output is capped, and concurrency stays at four or under so a run never becomes a load test.
A scheduled job probes every tracked endpoint every six hours and commits the raw result. Leaderboard figures come from a rolling 30-day window; older runs stay in the data and do not move the table.

Beyond single calls, the same Terminal-Bench tasks can run through two routers with Claude Code or Codex as the agent, verifier scores and costs side by side, with A/A and A/B statistics. These runs are hosted by our team on request.
A measurement that could not be taken is shown as missing, never as zero. Network latency from a scheduled runner is labelled as an estimate, and the probe region is printed on every figure.
Why a gateway company publishes a gateway benchmark

We sell a gateway, so a benchmark we run could be read as marketing. It is built so that it does not have to be trusted: the method is written down before the numbers, the raw data is public, and anyone can rerun it against the same endpoints with their own key. That is the same rule we hold our own products to.

Object storage is where AI data lives because it is cheap and durable. It is also slow to list, slow to open and poor at renames. Runix FS puts a file system and a cache in front of the bucket, and each mount picks how writes reach it: read-heavy data keeps the bucket as the source of truth, write-heavy work completes in Runix FS first and is synchronised to the bucket in the background.
A FUSE mount behaves like a local directory: open, read, write, rename and list. Tools such as git and inotify work against it unmodified.
Workers hold memory, SSD and HDD tiers and fill the fastest one with room first. Anything not cached is read straight from the bucket, and the cache fills in the background.
POSIX through FUSE, a Hadoop-compatible client for Spark and Flink, the native cv command line, and SDKs for Java, Python and Rust, all on the same files. FUSE, CSI or an SDK: which to use.
A CSI driver provisions ReadWriteMany volumes by creating a directory, not by calling a cloud API, so provisioning keeps up when thousands of pods start at once.
File paths map one-to-one to object keys. What is in your bucket keeps its original layout and stays readable by anything else, whether or not the cluster is running.
Metadata is replicated across masters with Raft, cached blocks can be replicated across workers, and a built-in web UI and metrics show every component.
Where it sits in your stack

Between the workloads that read data and the bucket that keeps it. Metadata goes to the masters; data is served by the workers, which read from the bucket on a miss and write back to it, directly or through a background sync depending on the mount mode.

Two mount modes. In cache mode the bucket is the source of truth and writes go straight to it. In file-system mode, the default, every operation completes in Runix FS first and is synchronised to the bucket in the background.
Four examples against the same namespace. Every command below is from the Curvine documentation; hosts and bucket names are placeholders.

Built for the workloads that stall on I/O
GPUs are the expensive part of an AI cluster, and they sit idle while data crosses the network one object at a time. These are the places where it shows up first.
Datasets and checkpoints are cached next to the GPU nodes, so epochs after the first read from the cache instead of the bucket, and checkpoints land on a file system instead of a multipart upload.
A shared tier for the KV cache that outlives a single GPU's memory, so a prompt prefix computed on one replica can be reused on another.

A post on the AWS Machine Learning Blog, written by AWS solutions architects with engineers from OPPO, where Curvine was started, walks through this on SageMaker HyperPod with Curvine as the shared tier and reports up to 2.7× faster time to first token at 2,500 tokens. Read the AWS post
Every agent wants its own writable workspace. Block volumes run into per-node attachment limits long before a node runs out of CPU; a directory on a shared file system does not.
The Curvine project provisioned 10,000 volumes for 10,000 agent pods on 99 EKS nodes, all bound and running, with a storage cluster of four pods. Read the write-up
Weights and artifacts are pulled once from the bucket and served from the cache to every node that starts a replica, instead of each node downloading the same files.
Spark and Flink read hot tables through the Hadoop-compatible client, with the cache absorbing repeated scans of the same files.
These figures are published in the Curvine project's README. They are not a Runix service level. During early access we measure on your data, your instances and your access pattern.

How is Runix FS related to Curvine?

Runix FS is built on Curvine, an open-source distributed file system and cache released under Apache 2.0 and accepted as a Cloud Native Computing Foundation Sandbox project. Runix deploys it into your cloud account and supports it under a contract with a US company.

In your own object storage. File paths map one-to-one to object keys, so what is in the bucket keeps its layout and stays readable without Runix FS. In cache mode the bucket is the source of truth and writes go straight to it; in file-system mode, writes complete in Runix FS first and reach the bucket through a background sync.
Do we have to change our code?

Usually not. Applications read and write through a FUSE mount as if it were a local directory, so training scripts keep working as they are. Hadoop-based jobs such as Spark use the Hadoop-compatible client, which takes configuration rather than code changes.
Which storage does it work with?
Amazon S3 and any S3-compatible store such as MinIO, plus Google Cloud Storage, Azure Blob Storage, Alibaba Cloud OSS and HDFS. The cluster runs on Kubernetes, on virtual machines or on bare metal.
During early access, pricing is quoted per deployment. Tell us how much data you have and what reads it, and we come back with a quote within one business day.
Can we buy it through AWS Marketplace?
Not yet. A listing is in preparation. Until then you contract directly with Runix AI Inc and are invoiced in USD.

What happens to one request
Your application holds one base URL and one key. This is everything Router does with a call, in order.
Your application sends the request to one Runix base URL with its key, in the OpenAI format it already speaks.

Runix Router checks the key: that it is active and not expired, that the call comes from an allowed IP, that the key may call this model, and that it has quota left. A call that fails a check is refused before it reaches a provider.
The request is forwarded to the provider that serves the model, and a streamed answer is passed through as it arrives, not buffered.
The tokens are metered at the model's price, and the response carries its usage, so a single call can be checked against the rate card.
The call is recorded in the request log with its key, model, tokens, cost and request id, which is what support traces a question with.
Your code holds the same base URL and key whichever model it calls. Changing models is a different string in the request, not a different integration.

From base model to production endpoint
One engagement, six pieces of work. Each produces something you can inspect: a dataset, a training run, an evaluation against your current model, an endpoint.
Supervised fine-tuning
Training on examples of the task done well: records your team has labelled, or a dataset built with Runix Data. The dataset is treated as the first step of the work, not an afterthought.
LoRA and QLoRA

Parameter-efficient tuning trains a small set of added weights instead of the whole model, which keeps training affordable. QLoRA does the same over a quantised base model, and adapters can be merged into the weights for serving.
Preference tuning
Direct preference optimisation (DPO) on pairs of better and worse answers, for behaviour that is easier to judge than to write down: tone, format, and when to decline.
Evaluation before rollout
Task-specific test sets held out from training, and a before-and-after comparison against the model you run today. A tuned model is only better if you can show it to whoever signs off.
Dedicated deployment

Single-tenant serving sized to your real traffic, in your cloud account or on capacity arranged per engagement, with upgrades and node failures planned for. Quantised variants only where the evaluation shows quality holds.

05 · Models
What we tune and serve

Licences, read first

Each family has its own terms. Some limit use above a number of monthly users, some require attribution or a naming convention for derived models, and some come with an acceptable-use policy. We read the licence against your use case before any work starts, and tell you if it does not fit.
Small and mid-size models

Models sized for one job done well: cheaper to serve on dedicated capacity, and practical to run inside your own account. Whether one is good enough for your task is what the evaluation is for, and we do not promise the answer in advance.
06 · Fit
When a tuned model is the right call
Not every team needs its own model, and we will say so if you do not: a hosted model through Runix Router is often the cheaper answer. These are the cases where a model of your own earns its cost.
The data cannot leave
A regulator, a customer contract or an internal policy rules out sending it to a shared inference service. A model that runs in your own account keeps prompts and outputs where the data already is.
The volume is steady and large
At constant, high volume, dedicated capacity stops being the expensive option, and a smaller model needs less hardware to serve it.
The task is narrow and repeated
Classification, extraction, routing or one well-defined kind of answer, asked many times a day. A tuned small model may be enough; the evaluation decides, and we tell you when it is not.
The model is the moat
You have tuned something on proprietary data, and it should run on your terms rather than someone else's.

02 · Definitions
What an agent in this layer is
Three definitions the rest of the page depends on.
What a domain agent is

A domain agent does the work of one profession, inside that profession's material: a coding agent in a repository, a studio agent in a script and its episodes. It is independent: it runs on its own and does not depend on the rest of the stack to do its job. What it produces is something a person in that domain already knows how to review.
What the harness is

The harness is what runs the agent: the loop that takes an instruction, plans the work, calls the model, applies the result to the material and stops where a person has to look. Each agent has its own, built for its domain, because the steps that make sense in a repository are not the steps that make sense in an episode.
Where the gateway sits

Runix Router is optional in front of an agent's model calls: one OpenAI-compatible endpoint, with keys, quotas and allowed models beneath it. The agent runs independently of it. Put Router in front when you want the agent's model usage governed and billed the same way as every other call.
03 · By domain
The agents, by professional domain
One agent per domain, each built around the tools, data rules, evaluation and review gate of that profession.
For engineering teams
Served today by Runix Code · An independent coding agent, reviewable in your repository

Runix Code is an AI coding agent being built for teams: grounded in your repository, with multi-file implement, refactor and test from one instruction, and every change landing as a reviewable diff. Seats, per-key limits and usage attribution by developer are part of it. In development, waitlist open.
Join the waitlist
Served today by Runix Comic · An independent agent for comic dramas, script to episode

Runix Comic is an AI studio agent for comic dramas being built around the whole job: scripts, episode plans, consistent characters and storyboards; styled panels, motion and camera, voice, music and subtitles; vertical cuts and full episodes for the platforms you name. In development, waitlist open.
04 · Next
Where the next agents come from
An agent needs its domain's rules before it needs a model. The Data layer already has rules for these four; none of them has an agent announced, and this page does not announce one.
The Data layer already has rules for finance data, with the public standards they follow. An agent for the domain would start from that same judgement; none is announced.

The Cybersecurity data rules →
Legal data has its own rules in the Data layer, with the public standards they follow. An agent in this domain is a candidate for the same reason; nothing is scheduled.
The Legal data rules →

The Data layer's work here is limited to biological data, antibody and protein records, with rules of its own. An agent would be a candidate only where that judgement is already in place; none is announced.
The AI for Science data rules →
05 · Principles
What every agent here must satisfy
Reviewable output

An agent's output is something a person in the domain reviews before it counts. Runix Code is built so every change lands as a reviewable diff, never a silent write; the same rule holds for every agent in the layer.
Grounded in your material

Runix Code works from your repository: its modules, idioms and the versions you run. Runix Comic works from your script, with characters that hold across scenes; neither starts from a tutorial's example.
Team controls

Seats, per-key limits and usage attribution by developer, as Runix Code is being built with, so an organisation can roll an agent out rather than discover it. The controls are set up with you, not left to the honour system.
Data terms in writing

Where Runix Router sits in front of an agent's model calls, its written data terms apply: content processed to serve the request, never used for training. The contracting entity is Runix AI Inc, with an MSA and a DPA on request.
06 · Questions
How many agents exist today?
Two: Runix Code for software engineering and Runix Comic for comic dramas. Both are in development and not generally available; their waitlists are open.
Does an agent need Runix Router?
No. Each agent runs independently, with its own harness. Router is optional in front of its model calls, for teams that want one endpoint, per-key limits and one itemised bill.
Will there be an agent for my domain?

Nothing beyond Code and Comic is announced, and no dates are published. The Data layer's six domains are where the domain judgement already exists, and waitlist cohorts set the order of what gets built.
Tell us which domain you work in

AI infrastructure engineers, obsessed with reliability

Our mission is to rebuild the operating system of AI, efficient, stable and enterprise-grade: Rebuild AI Unix. The name is the mission: Runix, from Rebuild and Unix. Runix Lab is the AI infrastructure brand of Runix AI Inc, a US-based technology company, and builds that system in five layers: storage (FS), data (Data and Pipeline), models (Models), a model gateway (Router), and the agents on top (Code and Comic), each an independent agent for its domain with its own harness.
02 · Company
The entity you would contract with, and what it actually operates today.

Runix AI Inc is a company incorporated in Wyoming, United States. It builds and operates infrastructure for teams putting AI into production, and sells it directly: there is no reseller between you and the people who run the service. The longer version of why it exists is Rebuild AI Unix. The original announcement from July 2026 is kept as a record of where the company started: a gateway and managed data pipelines, which became Router, Pipeline and Data. Where each product is today, and what comes next, is on the roadmap.
Eight products in five layers, at deliberately different stages. The statuses below are literal, and they are the same statuses used everywhere else on this site; none of them is aspirational.

Runix Router: available, with accounts opened by our team. One OpenAI-compatible endpoint across many providers, with central key custody, per-key quotas and allowlists, and a log of every request with its cost. What Router does.

Runix FS: early access, launched September 2026. A POSIX file system and multi-tier cache over the object storage a team already runs, built on the open-source Curvine project and deployed into the customer's own cloud account. What FS does.
Runix Models: early access, by engagement. Fine-tuning and dedicated serving of small and open-weight models, evaluated against the model a team runs today before anything ships. What Models does.
Runix Data: early access, by engagement. Training and evaluation data in six domains, with code as the focus, delivered with per-record provenance and licence and a quality report. What Data does.
Runix Pipeline, in development with design partners. The tooling behind Runix Data: ingestion, deduplication, schema-validated extraction, PII masking that fails closed. The six Pipeline stages.
Runix Code, in development, waitlist open. An AI coding agent for teams. Not generally available. Code and its waitlist.
Runix Comic, in development, waitlist open. An end-to-end studio for comic dramas. Not generally available. Comic and its waitlist.

03 · The thesis
Why one company builds all five layers, and why most teams start with one.
Every team is now an AI team, and none has an operating system

Model access, data preparation, tuning, storage and agents are bought from five vendors under five contracts, and the glue is scripts. The hard part of AI moved from the demo to the production run: keys, spend, failover, where prompts go, and what a model changed under you.
The wedge
Start with the layer that is on fire

Most teams arrive through the gateway: one endpoint, central keys, written data terms, available today. Some arrive through storage, because the bucket is starving their GPUs. The first layer earns the second; nothing requires the whole stack.
Why it compounds
Two paths, one set of interfaces

Requests go down through Router; data comes up through FS, Pipeline and Data into Models, which answer through Router again. Each layer is a product on its own, and each hand-off is an interface the team already uses, so the next layer arrives without a migration. Which layer, for which team.
04 · How we work
What we believe

The hard part of AI is not the demo: it is everything after: keeping services up when providers fail, keeping costs visible as usage grows, and turning messy data into something a model can actually use.
That is the work we love. Runix focuses on a small set of infrastructure problems and solves them properly, so the teams we serve can focus entirely on their product.
Reliability is a feature. We design for failure first and publish no availability number we have not yet earned.
Transparency builds trust. Clear pricing, itemized usage, honest communication.
Long-term over short-term. We would rather keep a customer for years than win a quarter.
Written down, not remembered. Decisions live in documents rather than in someone's head: which is also what working here is like.

05 · In the open
Three of the tools we built to run a gateway are open source, under CC0 or MIT. They work against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, including the ones we compete with.
Awesome AI Gateway
A decision tree over 160+ AI gateways, with a reproducible cost benchmark and a compliance and supply-chain scorecard behind every entry.
CC0, no vendor money and no affiliate links. Runix Router is deliberately not listed on it — a maintainer scoring their own product beside competitors is not a score worth reading. See the list.
A black-box benchmark for any gateway or relay: time-to-first-token, throughput, success rate, price multiple, plus fidelity probes for model echo, fake streaming and usage inflation.
Bring your own key and measure whoever you are evaluating — us included. Run the benchmark.
modelprobe
A dependency-free Go binary that reports, per model, whether it is up and how fast — one real but deliberately tiny call each.
Drop it in CI or a cron so an outage reaches you before it reaches your users. Get the prober.
06 · Not claimed
A short list, kept deliberately. Every item on it is something we could quietly imply and have chosen not to.
No badges we have not earned
Runix does not hold, and does not assert, SOC 2, ISO 27001 or PCI status.
If your procurement process requires one of these, say so early and we will tell you plainly where we stand rather than pointing at a roadmap. What we do document.
No published uptime figure
No uptime percentage, no availability chart, no historical graph.
Publishing a number means standing behind it, and the honest version of that commitment comes with a contract, not a marketing page. What Router does when a provider fails.
No logos, no invented case studies
You will not find a customer wall or a case study on this site.
